summary: This experimental document describes publicly logging TLS certificates as they are issued or observed, so anyone can audit certificate authority activity and spot suspect certificates. The intent is for clients eventually to refuse certificates not found in a log. It was later replaced by RFC 9162.

eli5.summary: Every ID card the internet hands out gets written in a public notebook, so anyone can spot a fake. A newer version has since replaced this.

questions: public ct logs for tls certificates
what is a signed certificate timestamp
how do i verify a certificate in a ct log
why are merkle trees used in certificate transparency
subtitle: Public audit logs for TLS certificates to detect misissued certificates.

tldr.problem: Certificate authorities can misissue TLS certificates without detection, allowing attackers to impersonate any website. Even after discovery, the damage is done and clients cannot easily prevent using the fake certificate.
tldr.mechanism: Certificate Transparency requires CAs to submit issued certificates to public, append-only logs. Certificates are assigned a Signed Certificate Timestamp (SCT) proving inclusion in a log; TLS clients verify the SCT and refuse certificates without one. Logs are audited using Merkle tree proofs to ensure they remain append-only.
tldr.outcome: Domain owners and security monitors can audit logs for unexpected certificates bearing their domains, and clients can trust that logged certificates have been audited. The protocol was later updated by RFC 9162, but this experimental version established the core approach.

facts.label: Signing algorithms
facts.value: ECDSA (NIST P-256) or RSA (2048 bits minimum)

facts.label: Maximum Merge Delay
facts.value: Log-defined; time within which submitted certificates must appear

facts.label: Log API
facts.value: HTTPS GET and POST with JSON responses

today: RFC 6962 is an Experimental protocol from June 2013 and has been obsoleted by RFC 9162. The core concepts of Certificate Transparency—public logs, SCTs, and Merkle tree auditing—remain the foundation of how deployed certificate transparency systems work, but RFC 9162 is the authoritative standard for new implementations.

sections.title: The Problem of Misissued Certificates
sections.content:
The internet relies on certificate authorities (CAs) to issue Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificates that prove a server is who it claims to be. If a CA issues a certificate to an attacker for a domain they don't own (a misissued certificate), the attacker can impersonate that domain, decrypt its traffic, and steal user credentials. Detecting and revoking misissued certificates is slow, and users who connected before revocation cannot know they were attacked.

RFC 6962 proposes Certificate Transparency: require CAs to log all issued certificates in public, auditable records. This way, domain owners can monitor logs for certificates they didn't request and take quick action. TLS clients can verify that a certificate has been logged and refuse certificates that have not been.
sections.eli5: Normally, if someone tricks a certificate maker into handing out a fake ID for your website, you don't find out until someone uses it to steal passwords. With Certificate Transparency, every ID handed out is written in a public notebook, so you can check it. If a fake one appears, you see it right away.

sections.title: Merkle Trees and Cryptographic Auditing
sections.content:
Logs store certificates in a Merkle Hash Tree, a structure where each node is the hash of its two children. The tree's root is a single hash that commits to all certificates in the log. When the log adds new certificates, it updates the root and signs it. This design allows anyone to prove that a certificate exists in the log using a short Merkle audit path (a list of sibling hashes), and to prove the log has only grown (not changed past entries) using a consistency proof.

The RFC specifies SHA-256 hashing and requires log operators to use either elliptic curve signatures (NIST P-256) or RSA with at least 2048 bits. Every log must issue a Signed Tree Head (STH)—a signature over the tree root, tree size, and timestamp—no older than the Maximum Merge Delay (MMD, the time within which new certificates must appear in the tree).
sections.eli5: Imagine a chain of sealed envelopes, each containing the fingerprints of all the certificates plus a summary of the previous envelope. If someone changes an old certificate, the chain breaks and everyone sees it. When you want to prove a certificate is in the log, you just show a few envelope fingerprints.

sections.title: Log Entries and Certificate Submission
sections.content:
A log entry consists of a TLS certificate chain (the end-entity certificate, any intermediate CAs, and the root CA). Anyone can submit a certificate, but logs only accept chains that lead to a trusted root CA they recognize. When a valid chain is submitted, the log immediately returns a Signed Certificate Timestamp (SCT)—a signature from the log promising to include the certificate in its Merkle tree within the MMD.

CAs can also submit Precertificates before issuing the final certificate. A Precertificate is a draft of the certificate with a special poison extension that makes it invalid as a real certificate. The log issues an SCT for the Precertificate, and the CA can later embed that SCT in the final, issued certificate. This allows the certificate to have an SCT from issuance onwards.
sections.eli5: You hand the log a certificate and a chain proving it's from a real certificate authority. The log checks the chain, writes down the certificate, and hands you a signed receipt (an SCT) that says 'I promise to list this by [date].' You can give that receipt to clients to prove you logged it.

sections.title: Integration with TLS and Client Verification
sections.content:
When a TLS server sends a certificate to a client, it must also include at least one SCT from a log. The SCT can be embedded in the certificate itself (as an X.509v3 extension), sent as a TLS extension during the handshake, or included in an OCSP response. TLS clients must verify the SCT signature using the log's public key and check that the SCT timestamp is not in the future. If a client receives a certificate without a valid SCT, it must reject the certificate.

Once a client has an SCT, it can later request a Merkle audit proof from the log to verify that the certificate actually appears in the log. This check can be asynchronous and need not reveal the exact certificate to the log (clients can batch requests for privacy). Logs provide several APIs: retrieve the current Signed Tree Head, fetch entries by index range, retrieve a Merkle proof by certificate hash, and verify consistency proofs between two tree snapshots.
sections.eli5: When a server hands you a certificate, it also hands you the signed receipt (SCT) from the log. Your browser checks that the receipt is real and not dated in the future. Later, you can ask the log 'is this certificate really in your notebook?' and the log gives you proof without knowing which certificate you're asking about.

sections.title: Monitoring and Auditing Logs
sections.content:
The RFC describes three types of log clients: Monitors regularly fetch all new entries from logs and can alert domain owners if unexpected certificates appear. Auditors take partial information about a log and verify it is consistent with other views by comparing Signed Tree Heads and requesting consistency proofs; any two conflicting STHs from the same log are cryptographic proof that the log misbehaved. Submitters (CAs and domain owners) submit certificates and use the returned SCTs to prove inclusion.

Logs can misbehave in two ways: failing to include a certificate with an SCT within the MMD, or violating the append-only property by showing different versions of the tree to different parties. Both are detectable. Gossip protocols (described separately) allow different parties to compare STHs and quickly spot a misbehaving log.
sections.eli5: Watchdogs monitor the logs, checking for certificates about your domain that you didn't request. If the log ever shows a different certificate list to different people, that's proof the log is lying, and everyone can see it because they share the signed summaries.

sections.title: Experimental Status and Future Evolution
sections.content:
This RFC is experimental and was published in June 2013 to allow evaluation and feedback. It specifies only SHA-256 hashing and fixed signature algorithms. The authors anticipated future revisions might add hash algorithm agility (allowing logs to specify their own algorithms), key rotation mechanisms, and gossip protocol specifications.

RFC 6962 was obsoleted by RFC 9162, which updates the protocol for standards-track deployment. The core mechanisms—logs, SCTs, Merkle trees, and auditing—remain unchanged, but RFC 9162 adds protocol flexibility and updates security considerations for real-world deployment.
sections.eli5: This was an experimental version released so everyone could test it and suggest improvements before making it a standard. A newer, better version (RFC 9162) came out later with the same basic idea but with improvements based on real use.

items.title: Merkle Hash Tree
items.text: All log entries hashed together into a single root hash, allowing proofs of inclusion and append-only verification.

items.title: Signed Certificate Timestamp
items.text: Log's cryptographic promise to include a submitted certificate within the Maximum Merge Delay.

items.title: Consistency Proof
items.text: Proof that an older version of the log is a complete subset of a newer version, preventing the log from rewriting history.

items.title: Audit Path
items.text: Short list of hashes needed to reconstruct the tree root and prove a certificate exists in the log.
